pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Earth Is Made of Rock

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** KS1 Y1 science 'Everyday materials' names **rock** as one of the everyday materials children identify and describe ('identify and name a variety of everyday materials, including wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, and rock') — a genuine hook for 'the ground is made of rock'. The broader Earth-structure content sits in KS2 Geography/science later.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 PE states 'Earth is made of rock' directly; it is foundational background for grade-2 ESS (Earth materials) and grade-4 ESS2 (the geosphere/surface processes). Treat as a conceptual foundation rather than an assessed PE at this age.

- **Operational details:** The big idea is that under the soil, grass and pavement, the Earth is solid rock — the whole planet is essentially a giant ball of rock. Two moves work at 5–7: (1) DIG DOWN — start at familiar ground (a garden, a beach) and go down through the thin layer of soil to bedrock, so children see soil is only a thin skin over rock; (2) ZOOM OUT — the stones and pebbles they hold are little pieces of that same Earth-rock. Handle real rocks and stones. Keep it to 'rock and other solid materials'; the hot interior, layers and core are the 7–9 'Earth's Layers' topic. This topic quietly underpins volcanoes (melted rock), rock types and earthquakes (rocks moving/breaking).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can state the ground is made of rock and that stones are pieces of the Earth; they are NOT yet expected to know layers or the hot interior. Confront 'the Earth is made of soil/dirt' (soil is a thin covering over rock) and 'the Earth is hollow'.
bestPractices: Handle real rocks, stones and pebbles — tie the abstract 'Earth is rock' to objects children can hold
Use a DIG-DOWN move (soil → bedrock) so children see soil is a thin skin over solid rock, correcting 'Earth is made of dirt'
Use a ZOOM-OUT move so a held pebble is understood as a small piece of the whole rocky Earth
Start from familiar local ground (playground, beach, garden) before generalising to the planet
Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer layers, heat and the core to the 7–9 'Earth's Layers' topic
Bridge to Y1 materials vocabulary ('rock' as an everyday material) so the idea sits in prior science
keyRepresentations: Dig-down cross-section: grass → thin soil → solid bedrock → deep rock
A held pebble shown as a tiny piece of a big rocky Earth (zoom-out)
Real rock/stone samples to handle and compare
A simple 'Earth is a ball of rock' globe cutaway (surface-level, no internal layers yet)
commonMisconceptions: 'The Earth is made of soil/dirt' — soil is only a thin covering; solid rock lies beneath almost everywhere
'The Earth is hollow inside' — it is solid rock and other materials all the way down (interior detail comes later)
'Rocks and the ground are different things' — stones are broken-off pieces of the same Earth-rock
'Only mountains/cliffs are rock' — rock is under flat ground and under the sea too, just often hidden by soil or water
'The ground is just made of the stuff on top (grass, sand)' — those are thin surface layers over rock

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: build the idea that if you dig deep enough beneath the soil, grass and pavement (sometimes also through sand, clay or gravel), you reach rock, that the Earth is made mostly of rock and other materials, and that stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock. Two complementary moves anchor the concept: DIG DOWN (from familiar ground through soil to bedrock) and ZOOM OUT (a held pebble is a tiny chip of the rocky planet). Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer layers, heat and the core to a later 'Earth's Layers' topic for 7–9s. Confront the common beliefs that the Earth is dirt/soil all the way down, that it is hollow, and that stones are separate from the ground.

activities.title: Dig down to the rock
feedback: If a child says soil or dirt continues all the way down: soil is only a thin skin at the top — dig deeper and you reach solid rock (bedrock). Show a soil-over-rock cross-section, or a photo of a deep excavation where diggers have gone down through the soil to the hard rock below (ordinary shallow digging may stay in soil, so use a deep-enough example).
If a child says the ground beneath is rock: good — point to how thin the soil band is compared with the thick rock below, so the idea of 'thin skin over rock' is clear.
Prompt to reinforce: 'If you dug down deep, far below the soil, what hard stuff would you reach?'
activities.rationale: A concrete dig-down from familiar ground to bedrock makes the abstract 'Earth is rock' visible and directly targets the 'Earth is made of dirt' belief by showing soil as a thin surface layer. A lift-the-flap or tap-to-reveal on the soil layer makes the 'thin skin over rock' idea concrete; these are optional ways to stage the reveal, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Beneath a thin layer of soil, solid bedrock underlies the land almost everywhere; soil is a thin surface covering
learnerActions: Start from a picture or cross-section of a familiar patch of ground — a garden, playground or beach.
Work down through the layers in order: grass, then a thin band of soil, then solid bedrock, then deeper rock.
Lift or reveal the soil layer to find the message underneath: 'just a thin skin — rock is underneath'.
Say aloud what is under the soil almost everywhere (rock), and how thin the soil is compared with the rock below.
Compare a real rock or stone in hand with the rock shown deep in the cross-section.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil is a thin covering compared with the rock beneath; dig deep enough (sometimes through sand, clay or gravel as well) and you reach solid rock almost everywhere, so the Earth is not dirt all the way down.

activities.title: Hands-on dig: how thin is the soil?
feedback: If the child expects to keep finding soil the deeper they dig: pause at the hard layer and name it — that is rock (bedrock). In the real ground this rock continues far deeper than the soil; in a tray or on-screen model the hard layer stands for that deep rock.
Encourage comparing the thin soil depth with the rock beneath so the 'thin skin' idea is felt, not just told.
activities.rationale: An active dig makes the discovery the child's own and is engaging at 5–7. A depth marker contrasting thin soil with deep rock makes the relationship concrete. This is an alternative route to the same recognition goal as the dig-down reveal; either can secure the idea. Because a tray cannot hold the real deep rock, treat it as a model of the ground.
sourceClaims: Beneath a thin layer of soil, solid bedrock underlies the land almost everywhere; soil is a thin surface covering
learnerActions: Use a trowel or digging tool — a soil tray set up as a model of the ground, or an on-screen dig — to remove soil until you reach something hard.
Mark or measure how deep the soil goes before you reach the hard layer.
Describe out loud: the soil layer is thin, and in the real ground the rock keeps going far below it (in the tray or screen, the hard layer stands for that deep rock).
Handle real rock, stone and pebble samples and compare them with each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing the soil yourself in a model shows the idea that soil is a thin layer sitting on top of much more rock below — the tray or screen is a model of the real ground, so it represents the real depths rather than measuring them.

activities.title: Zoom out: a pebble is a piece of the Earth
feedback: If a child treats a stone as just an object lying on the ground, separate from the Earth: a stone is a small broken-off piece of the Earth's rock.
Reinforce with the question: 'Is a stone you find on the ground a piece of the Earth, or something else?'
activities.rationale: Linking a held object to the whole planet (zoom-out) turns the abstract claim into something the child can connect to a thing in their hand, addressing the belief that rocks/stones are separate from the ground. A highlighted pebble linked to the globe view makes the connection concrete; this is an optional presentation choice.
learnerActions: Hold a real pebble or stone and look at a picture of the whole Earth as a planet made mostly of rock.
Zoom out from the dug-down ground to the whole planet, seeing it as an enormous ball made mostly of rock.
Point to the pebble and state that it is a tiny piece of the Earth's rock.
Decide and explain whether a stone found on the ground is a piece of the Earth or a separate object.
activities.intendedInsight: Stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock that have broken off and often been worn down — they are part of the Earth, not separate from it.

activities.title: Rock is everywhere, even where it's hidden
feedback: If a child thinks only mountains or cliffs are rock: rock is also under flat ground and under the sea, just hidden by soil or water.
If a child says the Earth is hollow or empty inside: it is full of rock and other materials, not empty. (Detail about the hot interior and layers comes in a later topic.)
Use the probe: 'Deep inside the Earth, is it empty or full of something? What?'
activities.rationale: Sorting can check how children classify materials and discussion surfaces where rock hides, confronting the 'only mountains are rock' and 'hollow Earth' beliefs; a sort alone checks classification but does not itself build the dig-down/zoom-out picture or elicit explanation, so pair it with talk. Keep claims to rock and other materials filling the Earth; do not introduce layers, heat or the core at this stage.
learnerActions: Sort pictures or objects into 'made of rock' and 'not made of rock'.
Discuss where rock is hidden: under flat grass, under sand at the beach, and under the sea — not only in mountains and cliffs.
Answer: 'What is under the soil almost everywhere?' (rock, not water or empty space).
Talk about what is deep inside the Earth: rock and other materials, not empty space.
activities.intendedInsight: Rock is beneath flat ground and under the sea too, often hidden by soil, sand or water; the Earth is full of rock and other materials, not hollow.

constraints: Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer Earth's layers, the hot interior and the core to the later 'Earth's Layers' topic for 7–9s.
This is a Tier A concrete/observational target: children should state the ground is made of rock and that stones are pieces of the Earth; they are not expected to know layers or the hot interior.

Sorting or multiple-choice questions can check 'what is under the soil?' and 'a stone is a piece of…', but on their own they do not build the dig-down and zoom-out mental picture; use them to check, not to introduce, the idea.
Handle real rocks, stones and pebbles where possible so the abstract idea ties to objects children can hold.
Start from familiar local ground before generalising to the whole planet.
Bridge to Year 1 'Everyday materials' vocabulary, where 'rock' is one of the named everyday materials, so the idea sits on prior science.

Lift-the-flap, tap-to-reveal, drag-to-dig, depth markers and highlighted pebbles are optional ways to make the reveal concrete; they are suggestions, not required mechanisms, and a fixed cross-section picture can still teach the idea.
A rotatable 3D globe adds only mild novelty for this recognition target and is not needed; a 2D cross-section conveys 'the ground is rock' clearly.
When using the builders'/digging example, present it as digging down deep enough to reach the hard rock beneath, not as a claim that ordinary house foundations always reach bedrock.
Any tray or on-screen dig is a model of real ground: the hard layer represents bedrock that continues far deeper than any tray; make this explicit so children do not take the tray bottom literally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The assessment's correctAnswer and one diagnostic answer mention 'very hot rock and metal' and a metal interior; these go beyond the stated 5–7 scope ('rock and other solid materials', with heat/layers/core explicitly deferred). Activities here avoid teaching the hot/metal interior to stay within the age target; retained only as background for adult reference.

The original row framed the reveal-based interactive as the single best delivery and rated open dialogue and 3D as poor/unnecessary. These are presentation preferences, not established efficacy claims; this rewrite keeps the dig-down and zoom-out as the core teaching moves while treating specific interaction styles as optional.

Claim that soil overlies bedrock 'almost everywhere' is reasonable as a general Earth-science statement but is sourced to an unverified general reference, and real soil depth varies widely; treat as a plausible simplification for this age, not a verified universal.

The inherited builders'-foundations example overstates the geology: ordinary foundations are usually dug into soil/subsoil and do not reliably reach bedrock. It has been reworded to illustrate 'dig deep enough and you reach rock'; do not teach that all foundations hit bedrock.
The hands-on dig uses a tray/on-screen model; this is noted inside the activity itself, since the hard layer only represents the real, far-deeper bedrock.

probeDeeper: Is the soil in a garden as thick as the whole Earth, or just a thin layer on top?
When builders dig down to lay foundations, what hard stuff do they hit?
Is a stone you find on the ground a piece of the Earth, or something else?
Deep inside the Earth, is it empty or full of something? What?
assess.correctAnswer: Just under the thin layer of soil at the top, it's mostly solid rock. The Earth is made of rock (and deeper still, very hot rock and metal). Soil is only a thin skin at the very top — the stones we find are pieces of that same rocky Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's dirt or soil all the way down
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil is a thin skin — dig deeper and you hit solid rock (bedrock); show a soil-over-rock cross-section or a photo of digging foundations.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would be soil or dirt all the way down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the deep hole stays in soil; no rock beneath.

errorPatterns.pattern: The Earth is hollow or empty inside
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Earth is solid rock and metal all the way through, not hollow.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would be hollow and empty inside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there's air or an empty space inside the Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rocks and stones aren't part of the Earth — they're separate things lying on it
errorPatterns.nextMove: A stone is a small broken-off piece of the same rock the Earth is made of.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that a stone is a piece of the Earth; treats it as just an object.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the Earth is dirt/soil all the way down, or hollow inside.
responseLevels.full: Explains soil is a thin top skin and beneath it the Earth is mostly solid rock, and recognises stones as pieces of that same Earth material.
responseLevels.partial: Says the ground is rock but imagines soil continuing far down, or is unsure what lies beneath the soil.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine you could dig a deep, deep hole straight down — much deeper than a garden. What would you find most of the way down, and what is the Earth mostly made of underneath us?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says 'the ground is rock' (first tier) may still imagine soil going all the way down. Asking what's DOWN THERE forces 'rock under the soil' — a child with the dirt misconception says soil or dirt continues all the way, and one with the hollow idea says it's empty inside.
